subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, show that (r₁ + r₂) sec²(C/2) = (r₂ + r₃) sec²(A/2) = (r₃ + r₁) sec²(B/2).

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.
formula_note: r₁ + r₂ = 4R cos²(C/2) is the building block behind the r + r₁ + r₂ − r₃ = 4R cos C family — multiplying by sec²(C/2) just cancels that cos²(C/2), leaving 4R alone. Each pair takes the half angle of the one vertex it excludes: r₁ + r₂ excludes r₃, so it uses C, not A or B.

steps.label: Simplify r₁ + r₂
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Both radii carry 4R cos(C/2), so it factors out — and the bracket left behind is sin((A+B)/2), which is cos(C/2).
steps.memory_tip: Both radii carry 4R cos(C/2), so it factors out, and the bracket left is sin((A+B)/2) = cos(C/2).
lines: (the formulas for r₁ and r₂ in half angles)
(sin X cos Y + cos X sin Y = sin(X + Y))

recall.must_convey: That 4R cos(C/2) factors out, the bracket becomes sin((A+B)/2) = cos(C/2), giving r₁ + r₂ = 4R cos²(C/2).

steps.why: sin((A+B)/2) = cos(C/2) because the two half-angles are complementary in any triangle. That is what turns one cos(C/2) into two.
common_mistakes: Grouping so that the C half-angle does not factor out.

steps.label: Multiply by sec² and conclude
steps.margin_note: The other half. sec²(C/2) is 1/cos²(C/2), so it cancels the cosine exactly, leaving 4R. The other two go the same way, so all three equal 4R.
steps.memory_tip: sec²(C/2) cancels the cosine exactly, leaving 4R. All three go the same way.

steps.why: Showing each equals the SAME thing is a cleaner proof than transforming one into another — and it is why 4R is worth computing rather than avoided.
common_mistakes: Proving only the first equality and stopping.
Writing sec² as cos² and multiplying instead of cancelling.

insider_note: Prove ONE of the three and say the others follow by rotating the letters. Each comes to 4R, and it is that shared value which makes them equal to one another.
